title: Understanding PSE students’ reactions to the postplagiarism concept: a quantitative analysis
extended_summary:
This paper examines how postsecondary education (PSE) students perceive “postplagiarism,” a framework proposed to reconceptualize academic integrity in response to generative AI. The central question is whether students accept the idea that GenAI is becoming a normal part of academic writing and whether they agree with related claims about creativity, attribution, responsibility, and the future of plagiarism definitions.

The study uses a cross-sectional quantitative survey built specifically for this project. Nineteen statements were derived from Eaton’s six tenets of postplagiarism and administered on a 4-point Likert scale to 581 PSE students residing in Australia, Canada, New Zealand, the United Kingdom, and the United States. Participants were recruited through Prolific, and most reported regular GenAI use. The instrument showed acceptable overall internal consistency, though several tenet-level subscales were weaker and suggested the need for refinement.

Findings show broad acceptance of hybrid human-AI writing, attribution, and policy adaptation, but also clear resistance around the idea that it is futile to distinguish human from AI-generated text, that AI enhances creativity without threat, and that humans can retain full control over writing in the age of AI. The paper concludes that institutions should not rely only on detection-based approaches; instead, they should develop nuanced policies and pedagogy that support ethical AI integration while preserving agency, creativity, and attribution norms.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic generative artificial intelligence tools used to generate, rewrite, or assist with text production and communication.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper examines PSE students’ perceptions of GenAI in academic writing, including hybrid human-AI writing, attribution, creativity, control, and plagiarism-related policy adaptation. It does not evaluate a specific product.

findings.finding_summary: In a cross-sectional survey of 581 postsecondary students across Australia, Canada, New Zealand, the United Kingdom, and the United States, 93.1% agreed that hybrid human-AI writing is becoming normal (PPM1), and 91.6% reported regular GenAI use. At the same time, 65.92% disagreed that it is futile to distinguish human- from AI-generated text (PPM3), 60.76% rejected the claim that AI does not threaten human creativity (PPM5), and 32.7% disagreed that humans can retain full control over what they write in the age of AI (PPM11).
findings.measure: Student agreement with 19 postplagiarism Likert-scale statements; survey responses on hybrid writing, creativity, human-AI distinction, and control

findings.finding_summary: The study found strong acceptance of GenAI-related policy adaptation and attribution norms: 95.1% agreed that citing, referencing, and attribution remain important (PPM17), and 90.0% agreed that policy definitions of academic integrity can and must adapt because of AI (PPM19). These results suggest students broadly support institutional adjustment to GenAI, even while expressing concerns about creativity and control.

quality_tier_rationale: This is a cross-sectional survey study with self-reported attitudes, not an experiment or meta-analysis. The instrument is newly developed and only preliminarily validated, so evidence is informative but not causal.
impact_tier_rationale: No effect sizes are reported, so impact cannot be quantified. Findings indicate broad acceptance of GenAI normalization and policy adaptation, but the study mainly reports perceptions rather than measured learning or performance impacts.
